title: Controlling Equational Reasoning in Large Language Models with Prompt Interventions
extended_summary:
This paper examines how prompt interventions can control specific mathematical error patterns in large language models (LLMs) performing equational reasoning. The authors are not studying a classroom or tutoring intervention; instead, they investigate how targeted perturbations to prompts affect derivation quality, hallucination rates, and error distributions in models such as T5, FLAN-T5, GPT-3.5/4, LLaMa-2, and Llemma.

The approach uses a symbolic data generation framework to create 30k fine-grained prompt-derivation pairs for a derivation generation task. The authors introduce four prompt interventions: variable renaming, expression exchange, alternative goal, and step removal. These interventions are applied to synthetic mathematical derivations and then evaluated through reference-based generation metrics, template-based error detection, and human assessment of derivation consistency and operator use. The work also compares fine-tuned T5/FLAN-T5 models with few-shot GPT and open-source models.

The paper’s key conclusion is that standard text generation metrics can be misleading for judging mathematical reasoning quality: they rank models differently from human and error-based evaluations. The authors find that fine-tuned FLAN-T5-Large and GPT-4 are strongest on in-distribution examples under human and surface-error analysis, while out-of-distribution perturbations reveal different weaknesses. Overall, the paper argues that specific prompt interventions correspond to identifiable error distributions, suggesting a way to control some categories of LLM mathematical hallucinations post-training.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed-style computational AI paper, but it is not an educational intervention study and has no K-12 participants, classroom setting, or counterfactual student outcome design. It provides methodological evidence only, so it does not meet RCT/QED criteria for the requested education evidence framework.
impact_tier_rationale: There is no direct impact on student achievement or schooling outcomes in grades 6–8. The reported gains are on synthetic LLM evaluation metrics and data-generation runtime, which do not translate to measurable educational impact for the target population.

interventions.use_case: LLM equational reasoning with targeted prompt interventions (variable renaming, expression exchange, alternative goal, and step removal) to probe and control mathematical error types in generated derivations; includes fine-tuning T5/FLAN-T5 and few-shot prompting GPT-3.5/GPT-4/LLaMa/Llemma on synthetic derivation tasks.

finding.finding_summary: This is not a K-12 instructional study and does not test student learning in grades 6–8. It evaluates LLM derivation quality on synthetic mathematical reasoning tasks, finding that fine-tuned T5/FLAN-T5 models can match or outperform few-shot GPT-4 on reference-based generation metrics, while human and template-based evaluation often favor GPT-4/FLAN-T5-Large on error counts; e.g., GPT-4 and FLAN-T5-Large each reached 98% in-distribution human-judged accuracy over 50 sampled derivations per model.
finding.measure: LLM derivation quality: ROUGE/BLEU/BLEURT/GLEU, template-based error counts, and human-judged equational reasoning accuracy
finding.study_size: n=750 human-evaluated derivations total; 50 static derivations per model plus 4 perturbed variants each

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports a symbolic data-generation framework that is approximately 15x faster than the prior version, reducing runtime from about 0.7 min/derivation to less than 0.05 min/derivation over 100 samples. This is an efficiency gain for dataset construction and evaluation pipelines, not a learner outcome.
finding.measure: Runtime per derivation in the symbolic data generation framework
